title: Describing motion: speed, velocity and acceleration

resources.label: PhET: Forces and Motion Basics
resources.note: The school recommends PhET. Push the crate and watch the speed readout.

steps.title: Distance and displacement
steps.body:
Walk 3 m east then 3 m west. You have travelled a **distance** of 6 m, but you are back where you started, so your **displacement** is zero.

Distance only has a size. It is a **scalar**. Displacement has a size *and* a direction: 3 m east is a different displacement from 3 m west. It is a **vector**.

Every quantity in this topic is one or the other, and the exam asks which. Speed is a scalar; velocity is the vector version. Time and mass are scalars; force and acceleration are vectors.

visuals.alt: A table of scalar quantities beside their vector partners: distance and displacement, speed and velocity, with time, mass and energy as scalars only and force and acceleration as vectors only

check.prompt: Which of these is a vector?
check.solution: Displacement has a direction, so it is a vector. The other three have only a size.

steps.title: Speed, and how fast things typically go
steps.body:
Speed is how much distance is covered each second. AQA expects you to know some **typical speeds**: a person walks at about 1.5 m/s, runs at about 3 m/s and cycles at about 6 m/s. Sound in air travels at about 330 m/s. Wind and traffic vary, but a car in town is around 13 m/s.

For something moving at a steady speed:

$$s = v\,t$$

$s$ is distance in metres, $v$ speed in m/s, $t$ time in seconds. This one is **not** on the equation sheet: recall it.

Most real journeys are not steady, so the speed you calculate from a whole journey is an **average** speed.

visuals.alt: A table of typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, car in town about 13 m/s, sound in air 330 m/s
A card showing distance travelled equals speed times time, with units m, m/s and s

check.prompt: A student walks at 1.5 m/s for 20 minutes. Calculate the distance walked, in metres.
check.solution: 20 minutes is $20 \times 60 = 1200$ s. $s = v t = 1.5 \times 1200 = 1800$ m.

steps.title: Rearranging for time or speed
steps.body: The same triangle of $s$, $v$ and $t$ gives all three forms: $v = s / t$ and $t = s / v$. Write the equation, substitute with units, then do the arithmetic. Marks are for the method, so a wrong final answer can still score.

visuals.problem: A cyclist rides at 6 m/s. How long does 900 m take?

steps.note: the unit follows from m divided by m/s
only convert if the question asks for minutes

check.prompt: A sound reaches you 2 s after a lightning flash. Sound travels at 330 m/s. How far away was the lightning?

steps.title: Velocity is speed with a direction
steps.body:
**Velocity** is speed in a stated direction. Two cars at 20 m/s, one heading north and one south, have the same speed but different velocities.

This matters for anything moving in a circle. A car going round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s has **constant speed** but its **velocity is changing all the time**, because its direction keeps changing. That is the example the exam uses.

When a question gives velocities in opposite directions, call one direction positive and the other negative. A ball thrown up at 5 m/s that comes back down at 5 m/s has changed velocity by 10 m/s.

visuals.problem: A satellite orbits Earth at a constant 7600 m/s. Is its velocity constant?

steps.text: Speed: the size, 7600 m/s, does not change
Direction: it is always turning, so the direction changes every second
Velocity is speed *and* direction, so the velocity is **changing** even though the speed is not
A changing velocity means the satellite is accelerating, towards the centre of the circle
steps.note: the same idea returns in Newton's laws

check.prompt: A runner goes once round a circular 400 m track at a steady 8 m/s. Which statement is correct?
check.solution: Speed is the same 8 m/s throughout. The direction changes all the way round, so the velocity changes.
options: Both speed and velocity are constant
Speed is constant but velocity changes
Velocity is constant but speed changes

steps.title: Distance-time graphs: gradient is speed
steps.body:
On a distance-time graph the **gradient** is the speed. A steeper line means faster; a flat line means stopped; a straight line means steady speed.

To find a speed, draw a triangle on the straight section and divide the rise (distance) by the run (time). On this graph the first stage rises 160 m in 20 s, so the speed is $160 \div 20 = 8$ m/s. The middle stage is flat: stopped for 15 s. The last stage is less steep, so slower.

A curved line means the speed is changing. The exam asks you to describe the motion stage by stage, using the words *steady speed*, *stationary*, *speeding up* and *slowing down*.

visuals.alt: A distance-time graph in three straight stages: rising from 0 to 160 m in the first 20 s, flat at 160 m from 20 s to 35 s, then rising to 220 m at 50 s, with a gradient triangle on the first stage labelled 8 m/s

check.prompt: Use the graph. What is the speed during the final stage, from 35 s to 50 s?
check.solution: Rise $220 - 160 = 60$ m over a run of $50 - 35 = 15$ s. Speed $= 60 \div 15 = 4$ m/s.

steps.title: Acceleration: how quickly velocity changes
steps.body:
**Acceleration** is the change in velocity each second:

$$a = \frac{\Delta v}{t}$$

$a$ is in metres per second squared (m/s²), $\Delta v$ is the change in velocity in m/s, $t$ the time in s. Recall this one too; it is not on the sheet.

$\Delta v$ is *final velocity minus starting velocity*. If it comes out negative the object is slowing down: a **deceleration**. An object falling freely near Earth accelerates at about **9.8 m/s²**, whatever its mass, if air resistance is small.

visuals.alt: A card showing acceleration equals change in velocity divided by time, with units m/s², m/s and s

check.prompt: A car's velocity increases from 3 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. Calculate its acceleration.

steps.title: When there is no time: v squared minus u squared
steps.body:
Some questions give a distance instead of a time. Then use the equation on the equation sheet:

$$v^2 - u^2 = 2\,a\,s$$

$v$ is the final velocity, $u$ the starting velocity, $a$ the acceleration, $s$ the distance. Write it out, substitute, then take the square root at the end. Forgetting the square root is the classic slip.

visuals.problem: A train starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s² over 100 m. Find its final velocity.

check.prompt: A ball is dropped and falls 5 m. Taking $g = 9.8$ m/s², what speed does it hit the ground at? Give your answer to 2 significant figures.
check.skill: using v squared minus u squared
check.solution: $v^2 = 2 \times 9.8 \times 5 = 98$, so $v = \sqrt{98} = 9.90$, which is **9.9 m/s** to 2 s.f.

steps.title: Velocity-time graphs: gradient and area
steps.body:
On a velocity-time graph two things are readable:

- the **gradient** is the acceleration
- the **area** under the line is the distance travelled

This graph shows an object reaching 12 m/s in 6 s, then holding 12 m/s for 4 s. The acceleration in the first stage is $12 \div 6 = 2$ m/s². The distance is the area: a triangle, $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 12 = 36$ m, plus a rectangle, $4 \times 12 = 48$ m, so 84 m in total.

Split any area into triangles and rectangles. A flat line at zero means stopped; a flat line above zero means steady speed, not stopped.

visuals.alt: A velocity-time graph rising in a straight line from 0 to 12 m/s over 6 s, then flat at 12 m/s until 10 s, with the triangle under the first stage shaded and labelled 36 m and the rectangle under the second shaded and labelled 48 m

check.prompt: Use the graph. What is the total distance travelled in the 10 s?
check.solution: Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 12 = 36$ m, rectangle $4 \times 12 = 48$ m, total $84$ m.

steps.title: Your turn: speed after a fall
steps.body:
Drag the height. The graph shows the speed an object reaches after falling that far from rest, from $v^2 = 2 g h$ with $g = 9.8$ m/s² and no air resistance.

Notice the shape: doubling the height does **not** double the speed, because it is $v^2$ that doubles. Falling 5 m gives about 9.9 m/s; falling 20 m gives about 19.8 m/s, twice the speed for four times the height.

visuals.fallback: A curve rising steeply at first and then more gently: about 9.9 m/s after 5 m, 14 m/s after 10 m, 19.8 m/s after 20 m, and 28 m/s after 40 m.

check.prompt: From $v^2 = 2 g h$ with $g = 9.8$ m/s²: an object falls 20 m. Find its speed to 3 significant figures.
check.skill: using v squared minus u squared

steps.title: Terminal velocity
steps.body:
Drop something through air and its velocity-time graph curves.

1. At first only weight acts, so it accelerates at about 9.8 m/s².
2. As it speeds up, **air resistance increases**. The resultant force downwards gets smaller, so the acceleration gets smaller: the graph curves over.
3. Eventually air resistance **equals** the weight. The resultant force is zero, the acceleration is zero, and the velocity stays constant. This is **terminal velocity**.

A skydiver reaches about 50 m/s, then opens a parachute: air resistance suddenly exceeds weight, the skydiver decelerates, and a new, lower terminal velocity is reached. The mark scheme wants *forces*, not just speeds.

visuals.alt: A velocity-time graph that rises steeply at first, curves over and levels off at a constant velocity marked terminal velocity, where air resistance equals weight

check.prompt: Why does a falling skydiver stop accelerating before the parachute opens?
check.solution: Air resistance increases with speed until it balances the weight. Zero resultant force means zero acceleration: constant velocity.

markScheme.description: air resistance equals weight, resultant zero

options: Gravity gets weaker the further they fall from the plane
Air resistance rises until it equals their weight
Their weight decreases as their speed increases
They have used up all of their kinetic energy

steps.title: Grade 9: speed from a curved distance-time graph
steps.body:
When a distance-time graph curves, the speed is changing, and the speed at one moment is the gradient of the **tangent** at that point. This is Higher-tier only, and it is where marks separate.

The curve here is an object accelerating steadily: its distance is $s = t^2$. To find its speed at 4 s, draw the straight line that just touches the curve at 4 s, then take the gradient of that line with a large triangle. The tangent passes through (2, 0) and (6, 32), so the speed is $32 \div 4 = 8$ m/s.

A large triangle reduces the error. Marks are given for a sensible tangent and for the working, so a reading between 7 and 9 m/s would score.

visuals.alt: A distance-time graph curving upwards, with a dashed tangent line touching it at 4 s that passes through the points 2 s, 0 m and 6 s, 32 m, and a gradient triangle on the tangent labelled 8 m/s

check.prompt: On the same curve $s = t^2$, a tangent drawn at 2 s passes through (1, 0) and (3, 8). What is the speed at 2 s?
check.solution: Gradient of the tangent: rise $8 - 0 = 8$ m, run $3 - 1 = 2$ s, speed $= 8 \div 2 = 4$ m/s.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Scalars have size only (distance, speed, time). Vectors have direction too (displacement, velocity, acceleration).
- $s = v t$ and $a = \Delta v / t$ are recall equations; $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$ is on the sheet.
- Distance-time graph: gradient is speed; a tangent gives the speed on a curve.
- Velocity-time graph: gradient is acceleration; area is distance.
- Typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, sound 330 m/s. Free fall: 9.8 m/s².
- Terminal velocity: air resistance grows until it equals weight, so the resultant force and the acceleration are zero.

visuals.alt: A card of the three motion equations: distance equals speed times time, acceleration equals change in velocity over time, and v squared minus u squared equals 2 a s

questions.prompt: A runner moves at a steady 3 m/s for 40 s. Calculate the distance covered.

questions.solution: Velocity is speed in a given direction, so it has a direction: a vector.

questions.prompt: A cyclist accelerates from rest to 12 m/s in 4 s. Calculate the acceleration.
Which is the best estimate of a person's walking speed?
questions.solution: Walking is about 1.5 m/s. 15 m/s is a fast car; 0.15 m/s is a slow crawl.

questions.prompt: The graph shows a distance-time graph for a bus. Use it to find the bus's speed in the first 30 s.
questions.solution: Gradient: rise $240$ m over run $30$ s. Speed $= 240 \div 30 = 8$ m/s.

visual.alt: A distance-time graph rising in a straight line from 0 to 240 m in 30 s then flat to 45 s

questions.prompt: The velocity-time graph shows a car reaching 10 m/s in 5 s and then travelling at 10 m/s for a further 10 s. Calculate the total distance travelled.
questions.solution: Area under the graph. Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 10 = 25$ m. Rectangle $10 \times 10 = 100$ m. Total $125$ m.

visual.alt: A velocity-time graph rising from 0 to 10 m/s in 5 s then flat at 10 m/s until 15 s

questions.prompt: A car accelerates from rest at 2.5 m/s² over a distance of 80 m. Calculate its final velocity.
questions.skill: using v squared minus u squared

questions.prompt: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
questions.solution: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the **acceleration**. The area under it is the distance.
accepted: the rate of change of velocity

questions.prompt: A train travelling at 30 m/s brakes to a stop in 6 s. Calculate its deceleration.
questions.solution: $\Delta v = 0 - 30 = -30$ m/s. $a = -30 \div 6 = -5$ m/s², a deceleration of 5 m/s².

questions.prompt: A car drives round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s. Which is true?
questions.solution: Steady speed, but the direction is changing all the time, so the velocity changes. A changing velocity is an acceleration.
options: Its velocity is changing because its direction changes

questions.prompt: A car travelling at 25 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 6.25 m/s². Calculate the distance it travels while stopping.
questions.skill: rearranging v squared minus u squared

questions.prompt: A skydiver jumps from a plane and falls for some time before opening a parachute. Describe and explain how the skydiver's velocity changes, from the moment of jumping until landing. Refer to the forces acting.
questions.solution: Straight after jumping, only weight acts (air resistance is zero), so the resultant force is the weight and the skydiver accelerates at about 9.8 m/s². As velocity increases, air resistance increases, so the resultant force downwards decreases and the acceleration decreases. When air resistance equals weight the resultant force is zero and the velocity is constant: terminal velocity. Opening the parachute increases the area, so air resistance suddenly exceeds weight; the resultant force is upwards and the skydiver decelerates. As velocity falls, air resistance falls until it again equals weight, giving a new, lower terminal velocity for a safe landing.

markScheme.description: at first only weight acts, so accelerates
air resistance increases with speed, so resultant force and acceleration decrease
air resistance equals weight: resultant zero, constant velocity
parachute increases air resistance above weight, so decelerates
new lower terminal velocity when forces balance again

criteria.text: Only weight acts at the start, so the skydiver accelerates (at about 9.8 m/s²)
Air resistance increases as speed increases, reducing the resultant force and the acceleration
Air resistance becomes equal to weight, so resultant force is zero and velocity is constant
This constant velocity is called terminal velocity
Opening the parachute makes air resistance greater than weight, so the resultant force is upwards and the skydiver decelerates
Air resistance falls until it equals weight again, giving a lower terminal velocity

questions.modelAnswer: At the moment of jumping the skydiver's velocity is zero, so there is no air resistance and the only force is weight. The resultant force equals the weight, so the skydiver accelerates downwards at about 9.8 m/s². As velocity increases, air resistance increases. The resultant force (weight minus air resistance) gets smaller, so the acceleration gets smaller, though the skydiver is still speeding up. Eventually air resistance equals weight. The resultant force is zero, so there is no acceleration and the velocity is constant. This is terminal velocity, roughly 50 m/s. When the parachute opens, its large area makes air resistance much bigger than weight. The resultant force is now upwards, so the skydiver decelerates. As the velocity drops, air resistance drops, until it once again equals weight. The skydiver then falls at a new, much lower terminal velocity and lands safely.

questions.prompt: The velocity-time graph shows a lift: it accelerates from rest to 8 m/s in 4 s, travels at 8 m/s for 6 s, then decelerates to rest in 2 s. Calculate the total distance travelled.
questions.solution: Three areas. Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 8 = 16$ m. Rectangle $6 \times 8 = 48$ m. Triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 8 = 8$ m. Total $72$ m.

visual.alt: A velocity-time graph: a straight rise from 0 to 8 m/s in 4 s, flat at 8 m/s until 10 s, then a straight fall to 0 at 12 s

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from a bridge 20 m above a river. Air resistance can be ignored and $g = 9.8$ m/s². Show that the stone hits the water at just under 20 m/s.
questions.skill: show-that with v squared minus u squared
questions.solution: $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$ with $u = 0$: $v^2 = 2 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 392$. $v = \sqrt{392} = 19.8$ m/s, which is just under 20 m/s as required.

markScheme.description: 19.8 m/s, with the comparison to 20 m/s stated

criteria.text: Selects $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$ and sets $u = 0$
19.8 m/s and states this is just under 20 m/s

questions.modelAnswer: The stone starts from rest, so $u = 0$. Using $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$: $v^2 = 2 \times 9.8 \times 20 = 392$. Taking the square root, $v = 19.8$ m/s (to 3 s.f.). This is just under 20 m/s, as required.

questions.prompt: The distance-time graph shows an accelerating object. A tangent drawn at 3 s passes through the points (1 s, $-4.5$ m) and (5 s, 31.5 m). Use the tangent to find the speed at 3 s.
questions.solution: Gradient of the tangent: rise $31.5 - (-4.5) = 36$ m, run $5 - 1 = 4$ s, so speed $= 36 \div 4 = 9$ m/s.

visual.alt: A distance-time graph curving upwards with a dashed tangent touching it at 3 s; the tangent passes through 1 s, minus 4.5 m and 5 s, 31.5 m

questions.prompt: A student walks 600 m to a bus stop at 5 m/s, then rides 900 m on a bus at an average of 15 m/s. Calculate the average speed for the whole journey. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.solution: Time walking $= 600 \div 5 = 120$ s. Time on the bus $= 900 \div 15 = 60$ s. Total distance 1500 m in 180 s. Average speed $= 1500 \div 180 = 8.33$ m/s. Not the average of 5 and 15.

questions.prompt: A velocity-time graph is curved. Put the steps for estimating the distance travelled in order.
questions.solution: The distance is the area, so find the value of one square first, count whole squares, estimate the part squares, then multiply.
items: Work out what one grid square is worth: its height in m/s times its width in s
Count the whole squares under the curve
Add the part squares, counting each as about half
Multiply the total number of squares by the value of one square

questions.prompt: An aircraft on a runway is moving at 20 m/s when its engines give it an acceleration of 3 m/s². It travels a further 400 m before taking off. Calculate its take-off velocity. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
questions.skill: using v squared minus u squared with a non-zero start

questions.prompt: The graph shows two cars over 20 s. Car A accelerates from rest to 20 m/s in 10 s, then stays at 20 m/s. Car B travels at a constant 15 m/s throughout. A student says: *Car A must travel further, because it is going faster at the end.* Evaluate this claim, using calculations.
questions.skill: evaluating a claim with velocity-time graphs
questions.solution: Distance is the area under a velocity-time graph. Car A: triangle $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ m plus rectangle $10 \times 20 = 200$ m, total 300 m. Car B: $20 \times 15 = 300$ m. The distances are equal, so the claim is wrong: being faster at the end does not mean travelling further, because A was slower than B for the first 7.5 s.

markScheme.description: distance is area under the graph
equal distances, so the claim is wrong
reason: A was slower than B for the first 7.5 s, which cancels its later advantage

criteria.text: Uses area under the graph for distance
Concludes the distances are equal, so the claim is wrong
Explains why: A was slower than B until 7.5 s, so its later speed only makes up the gap

questions.modelAnswer: The distance each car travels is the area under its line. Car A: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 20 = 100$ m while accelerating, then $10 \times 20 = 200$ m at constant velocity, so 300 m in total. Car B: $20 \times 15 = 300$ m. The two distances are equal, so the student is wrong. Car A is faster at the end but was slower than B for the first 7.5 s (until its velocity passed 15 m/s), and the distance it lost then is exactly made up later. The final speed alone says nothing about the distance; only the area does.

visual.alt: A velocity-time graph with two lines: car A rising from 0 to 20 m/s over 10 s then flat at 20 m/s to 20 s, and car B flat at 15 m/s throughout

examTechnique.body:
Motion questions are mostly graphs and three equations, and the marks are lost on habits rather than ideas. Say which graph you are reading before you read it: gradient is speed on a distance-time graph and acceleration on a velocity-time graph, and only a velocity-time graph has a useful area. Write the equation, substitute with units, then calculate; with $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$, take the square root last and say so.

Describing motion from a graph is a *stage by stage* job: name each section with *steady speed*, *stationary*, *accelerating* or *decelerating*, and give a number where you can. The Year 9 Milestone re-tests all of this alongside Hooke's law and moments, so it is worth keeping sharp.
examinerErrors: Giving $v^2$ as the answer. 400 is the square of the velocity; the velocity is 20 m/s.
Reading the area under a distance-time graph. It means nothing; only the gradient does.
Averaging two speeds to get an average speed. Average speed is total distance divided by total time, and the slower stage takes longer.
Describing a flat line above the axis on a velocity-time graph as *stopped*. It is steady speed; stopped is a flat line at zero.
Explaining terminal velocity with speeds only. The marks are for *air resistance increases until it equals weight, so the resultant force is zero*.
Calling speed a vector, or velocity a scalar. Speed is a scalar; velocity is the vector.
Reading a curve's speed from a chord or from the origin instead of drawing a tangent at the point asked for.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the graph before reading it, draws a large gradient triangle or tangent and shows the rise and run, and splits an area into labelled triangles and rectangles with each part's value written down. It carries $u$ through $v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s$ when the start is not from rest, takes the square root last, and gives a sensible number of significant figures. In explanations it argues from forces to acceleration to velocity, in that order, and it can show with a calculation that a claim about a graph is wrong.
